slides.title: The role of laboratory medicine and directions of its development
bullets: As a teaching discipline, clinical laboratory diagnostics teaches how to determine the relevant parameters of biological material to assess the functional state of the body’s physiological systems.
It addresses early and differential diagnosis, confirmation of treatment effectiveness, and prognosis of the course and outcome of disease.
At the molecular level it studies the pathogenesis of diseases, their complications and outcomes.
The discipline grew out of clinical biochemistry and biological chemistry, so a large share of laboratory tests are done by biochemical methods.
Laboratory diagnostics is developing rapidly worldwide through automation and the introduction of new methods; this speeds up diagnosis in both urgent and planned care.
A physician working with laboratory tests must know the methodological details of handling biological material and interpret results correctly.

slides.title: Recommended tests for a primary-care laboratory (rural doctor’s post example)
bullets: The manual was written for the clinical diagnostic laboratories of rural doctor’s posts (RDP); its methods follow the Ministry of Health’s mandatory minimum of laboratory tests for RDPs.

As its basis, it quotes an extract from Ministry of Health order No. 170 of 13 April 2000 “On improving laboratory diagnostics and strengthening the material and technical base of the laboratories of treatment and prevention institutions”.
Biochemical minimum: ALT, glucose, bilirubin and its fractions, urea (test systems, photometric method).

General clinical minimum: haematology (ESR, leukocytes, haemoglobin); urine (volume, relative density, colour, clarity and sediment, protein, qualitative glucose, ketone bodies, blood, bilirubin, reaction pH); stool (shape, inclusions, mucus, pH, consistency, colour, odour, occult blood).

slides.title: Recommended tests for a primary-care laboratory (rural doctor’s post example)
bullets: RDP laboratories are staffed by technicians with secondary medical education and receive material from patients with very different problems, so the methods must be informative, multi-purpose and methodologically simple.
The manual has three chapters: biochemical methods, general clinical methods and recommendations for internal quality control.

slides.title: Laboratory automation and information systems
bullets: The growing range and number of laboratory parameters call for better organisation and technology in the laboratory: automated instruments, special analytical systems and computers are introduced.
First direction — processes inside the laboratory: registering biological material, distributing orders among laboratory sections, recording and issuing results, analysing activity.
Automating the analysis: entering and processing data from analysers, checking and controlling instrument operation.
Quality control and accounting: locating errors by their source, assessing the accuracy and trueness of results and processing them statistically; keeping track of reagents and equipment.
Second direction — linking the laboratory to the hospital information system: ordering tests and receiving results through terminals in clinical departments, building a data bank.

slides.title: Laboratory automation and information systems
bullets: Goals: raise the quality and efficiency of testing, control consumption, cut unnecessary manual work, and support the physician’s decisions (fewer unjustified tests, correct interpretation of results).

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
rows: x̄ and SD from at least 20 measurements on different days measurement

slides.title: Control material prepared from horse serum can be used in the following cases:
options: turbidity less than 0.2 units. Extinction (cuvette 0.3 cm; wavelength 630–690 nm)

slides.title: Not used in quality control of coagulation tests:
options: Fresh pooled plasma from many donors (at least 20 people), standard lyophilized human plasma for calibration
plasma prepared from human plasma with a precise concentration of coagulation factors (normal and pathological)
control plasma deficient in some coagulation factors
Fresh plasma obtained from a donor

slides.title: Quality management method that does not require control materials:
options: Study of parallel samples, repeat testing of the sample

slides.title: Interlaboratory quality control makes it possible to:
options: Compare the quality of work of several laboratories
Assess the quality of the methods used

slides.title: It is proposed to use the following for quality control of biochemical tests:
options: ready-made commercially produced serum (liquid or lyophilized)

slides.title: General rules for quality control of clinical laboratory tests?
bullets: 1. The quality assurance system covers the entire testing process (pre-pre → preanalytical → analytical → postanalytical → post-post); the standard is ISO 15189:2022.

2. Internal quality control: in each run (at least daily) control materials at two or more levels, Levey–Jennings charts and Westgard rules; if a run is not accepted, patient results are not released, the cause is found, corrected and recorded.
3. External quality assessment (interlaboratory comparison, PT) – regular participation, analysis of results and corrective actions.
4. Equipment and reagents: calibration, preventive maintenance, temperature control, checking reagent lots and expiry; method verification/validation.
5. Staff competence, SOPs, documentation and traceability; quality indicators (specimen rejection, turnaround time, critical value notifications) and internal audits.

slides.title: Quality of laboratory tests and the factors affecting it?
bullets: 1. The quality of a laboratory result is its fitness for a clinical decision: trueness (absence of systematic error), precision/repeatability (small random error), timely release, correct interpretation.
2. Preanalytical factors (more than half of errors): incorrect ordering, patient preparation, identification errors, wrong tube, hemolysis, clot, low volume, transport and storage.

3. Analytical factors: calibration, reagent quality and expiry, instrument malfunction, interferences (hemolysis, lipemia, bilirubin, drugs), staff qualification; detected by internal and external control.
4. Postanalytical factors: incorrect entry/transmission of the result, wrong unit or reference interval, failure to report a critical value, delay.
5. Biological factors: age, sex, circadian rhythm, pregnancy, diet, physical exertion – taken into account in reference intervals and interpretation.

slides.title: Principles of quality control of clinical laboratory tests?
bullets: 1. Basic principles: control applies to the entire testing process, is regular and documented, statistically based, and aimed at preventing and correcting errors (continuous improvement).
2. Control materials should have a matrix similar to the patient sample, concentrations close to clinical decision levels, and be independent of the calibrator.
3. Statistical control: the mean (x̄), standard deviation (SD) and coefficient of variation (CV%) are determined; acceptance/rejection of a run by the Levey–Jennings chart and Westgard multirules.
4. External control assesses trueness (bias); method performance is compared with quality requirements.
5. For each nonconformity – corrective and preventive actions, records and staff training (ISO 15189).
